turns.query: Use the retrospective September 30, 2025 FFIEC 041 domestic-office RC-E time-deposit maturity/repricing data and same-date FDIC financials, matching the reported FDIC certificate. Keep banks with complete nonnegative RC-E amounts, FDIC assets above USD 5 billion, positive cash, positive combined true one-year time-deposit maturities, and a positive combined excess of one-year maturity-or-repricing buckets over those true maturities. Rank that excess descending, RSSD ascending for ties. Report the eligible count and leading RSSD ID. Explain the difference between a time deposit resetting its rate and one maturing.

claims.description: The response distinguishes a rate reset on a continuing time deposit from contractual principal maturity and cash repayment.

turns.query: For that bank, separately report the one-year maturity-or-repricing bucket and the true one-year contractual-maturity amount for time deposits of at most USD 250,000 and for those above USD 250,000, in USD millions. Interpret the excess in each size class.

claims.description: The response identifies the material over-USD-250,000 bucket excess as deposits that can reprice within one year while contractually maturing later, rather than an extra one-year cash outflow.

turns.query: Carry both size classes forward to a one-year planning horizon. Assume exactly half of deposits contractually maturing within the year renew at maturity and half leave; all departures are paid from opening FDIC cash, with no other cash flows. Assume a 150-basis-point rise applies in full to the retained later-maturing deposits that reset within the year and to the renewed deposits. Report ending cash and the next-year annualized incremental interest expense, in USD millions. Explain the relationship between these cash and interest-cost effects. Treat this as a hypothetical run-rate after all resets and renewals, not interest accrued during the planning year.

claims.description: The response keeps later-maturing reset deposits in the interest-cost base without counting them as principal cash outflow, and treats renewal as retaining principal at a higher hypothetical rate.

turns.query: Replan from the same opening bank and deposits, replacing the half-renewal assumption. Require at least USD 100 million of cash after all one-year contractual maturities; a common fraction of both size classes renews and the rest leave. With no borrowing or other flows, find the smallest feasible renewal percentage. Report its next-year annualized incremental interest expense under the same 150-basis-point pass-through. Carry unrounded amounts through the calculation and compare the cash-cost tradeoff with the prior plan.

claims.description: The response recognizes that retaining slightly more maturing deposits than in the half-renewal branch protects the stated cash floor but raises the annualized interest-cost run-rate.

judge_reference.source: Frozen 2025Q3 FFIEC 041 RC-E domestic-office time-deposit memorandum fields and same-date FDIC BankFind cash/assets; all renewal and 150 bp pricing terms are hypothetical.
facts: The eligible sample contains 86 banks and the largest observed long-maturity/near-reset excess belongs to RSSD 673440.
Its at-most-USD-250,000 short bucket and true maturities are 709.935 and 709.412 million USD; the over-USD-250,000 amounts are 804.584 and 372.448 million USD.

At 50 percent renewal, cash ends at 72.091 million USD and next-year incremental interest expense is 14.6038 million USD. An exact 100 million USD cash floor requires 52.5797 percent renewal, with 15.0225 million USD next-year expense.
known_overclaims: Treating the entire mixed reset-or-maturity bucket as contractually due within one year.
Calling the 150 bp pass-through observed bank pricing or recognizing a full year of interest expense during the planning year.
Using the 50 percent branch's remaining cash as the opening cash for the final replanning branch.
